analysis.one_liner: Bans PACs and soft money from federal elections, tightens FEC enforcement, and gives challengers party seed money.
analysis.headline: Sponsored and cosponsored by 25 of 44 Senate Republicans in January 1993, the bill was referred to the Senate Rules Committee, received one hearing on March 3, 1993, and died there without a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited political action committees from contributing to or spending on federal elections, and banned 'soft money' — the unlimited, undisclosed money flowing to party committees from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors. It would have stiffened FEC penalties and speeded enforcement, required broadcasters to give candidates un-preemptible ad time at the lowest rate, limited gerrymandering and taxpayer-funded mass mailings by incumbents, and let national party committees give up to $100,000 in seed money to challengers. It also modestly raised and indexed individual contribution limits. It never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would have seen less special-interest money and fuller disclosure in federal elections; challengers, who would have had access to party seed money and faced fewer incumbent advantages (franked mail, safe gerrymandered districts); and the Federal Election Commission, whose enforcement powers would have been strengthened.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person other than an individual or a candidate/party political committee from contributing or spending to influence a federal election — eliminating corporate, union, and trade-association PACs.

Bans soft money: money raised outside FECA's source restrictions, limits, and disclosure rules becomes unlawful for influencing any federal election, with allocation and disclosure rules imposed on party committees.

Strengthens FEC enforcement: mandatory minimum penalties (up to 200-300% of the contribution for knowing violations), injunctive authority, 60-day deadlines, and a private right of action for candidates when the FEC deadlocks.
Gives national party campaign committees power to contribute up to $100,000 in seed money to federal candidates who do not hold office, matched to their in-state fundraising.

Requires declaration and disclosure when candidates spend more than $250,000 of their own or immediate family money, triggering higher contribution limits for opponents; limits franked mass mailings during election years; sets compactness and anti-dilution standards for congressional redistricting with judicial enforcement.

Prohibits broadcast licensees from preempting candidate ad time purchased during the 45 days before a primary and 60 days before a general election, and requires prominent disclosure of who paid for independent-expenditure ads.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees funded by corporations, labor unions, and trade associations would be eliminated from federal elections; national and state party committees would lose soft-money fundraising and face allocation and disclosure rules; broadcasters would have to honor candidate ad purchases without preemption; and tax-exempt organizations engaged in federal campaign activity would lose tax-exempt status.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the individual contribution limit and indexes it to inflation, shifting more of the financing burden onto large individual donors — a trade-off Republicans framed as replacing PAC money, but one that favors candidates with access to wealthy givers.

It denies tax-exempt status to organizations that engage in federal campaign activity or run voter registration drives when candidates have solicited for them, provisions that could burden civic and issue organizations on both sides.

It imposes detailed conditions on labor organizations' political activities, including fee computation, independent audits, and challenge procedures — conditions not mirrored for corporate political spending, which the bill addresses only through the overall PAC ban.

Its redistricting standards (compactness, no intent to dilute a party's voting strength) are constitutionally contested, and courts might have struck parts of the bill; the bill includes a severability clause anticipating that outcome.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked the two largest channels of special-interest money — PACs and soft money — and paired the ban with stronger enforcement and real help for challengers, which most reform advocates would count as a net gain for ordinary voters. The serious trade-offs are that it substitutes somewhat higher individual limits for PAC money (a benefit concentrated among candidates who can attract large donors) and that several provisions targeting tax-exempt groups and unions carry risk of being used against legitimate civic activity. The single-party sponsorship also meant it functioned as a partisan alternative to the Democratic majority's own reform bill rather than a negotiated bipartisan plan.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Rules and Administration Committee for the whole two-year Congress: one hearing in March 1993, then no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Dole and 13 other Republican senators introduced the bill on January 21, 1993, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
The Rules Committee held hearings on March 3, 1993, but never reported the bill.
No further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 103rd Congress, which ended January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, party soft-money operations, tax-exempt political spenders, and incumbent officeholders all kept the status quo: unlimited undisclosed party money stayed legal for another decade, and no seed money or competition provisions arrived for challengers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs, party soft money, and incumbents

for.name: Sen. Robert J. Dole
for.what_they_did: Introduced S.7 on January 21, 1993, with introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Wendell Ford, D-KY)
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on March 3, 1993, then never marked up, reported, or scheduled the bill.

against.name: George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor agenda and never brought S.7 to the floor; the majority pursued its own campaign finance bill (S.3) instead.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 supporters (sponsor plus 24 cosponsors) were Republicans — 24 of 44 Senate Republicans — and no Democrat cosponsored it; the Democratic majority referred it to its Rules Committee and never reported it.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, union, and trade-association PACs)
industries.note: The bill eliminates PAC contributions and spending in federal elections entirely, cutting off the main direct funding channel from organized business and labor to candidates.
Parties lose soft-money fundraising and face strict allocation and disclosure rules, but gain new powers: seed money for challengers, higher indexed limits, and expanded party contribution authority.
Organizations participating in federal campaigns, or running registration drives solicited by candidates, would lose tax-exempt status, removing a vehicle for undisclosed political spending.
Stations could no longer preempt candidate ad purchases in preelection windows and must honor lowest-unit-charge rates, modestly reducing their scheduling flexibility and rate-setting power.
